chapter: New Orleans bands, Oliver and Armstrong
title: Armstrong as first great soloist; Rose listens for the band
summary: Asked about Gunther Schuller's claim, Rose half agrees. He says he hears solos as an intermission because he listens for the band.

story.theme_name: Working with and around Louis Armstrong
story.community_name: Playing with and around Louis Armstrong

blocks.x: All right. So, that's interesting. So, of course, people like Gunther Schuller, who wrote the most recent book on jazz, which he called Early Jazz, called Louis the First Great Soloist. And I guess he was referring to him as a first great jazz soloist. You would agree with that, that he would be the first great jazz soloist?

I suppose I would agree with that, although, as a matter of fact, I never really thought that much about solos. As I mentioned to you earlier, not in this interview, but my own approach to most things is really very narrow. And for my ear, in listening to jazz, a solo is mainly an intermission. And it is very difficult for me to even pay attention to what a soloist is doing, because I am listening for the band. Now, that's a peculiarity of my own musical tastes and interest, and is not one which I particularly recommend or defend for general use. But irrespective of the taste factor that's involved there, the fact of the matter is that the tradition of the jazz did not include extended solo as part of the form.
